meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 15: Versioning, Changelog & Lifecycle
meta.revision: v2.1 (curated 2026-09-12, 200 items, verified against the 2026-07-28 specification)

questions.question: A modern-only client connects to a legacy-only server. What does version negotiation achieve?

options.text: It downgrades the client to the legacy handshake automatically
It succeeds if both sides support at least one common revision date
Nothing beyond detecting the mismatch: it does not bridge the two eras
It upgrades the server, which must answer modern requests once asked

questions.explanation: Negotiation detects mismatches; it does not translate between eras. A modern client facing a legacy server fails, which is why dual-era clients probe first (server/discover on stdio, or inspecting a 400 body on HTTP) and fall back to initialize themselves.

questions.question: What is the minimum time a feature stays Deprecated before it may be removed, and when can that floor be shortened?

options.text: One revision, since removal happens in the next Current revision unless an extension is granted
Twelve months, shortened only for an active security risk, and never below ninety days
Twelve months, shortened whenever the Core Maintainers agree unanimously
Six months, extended to twelve if a Tier 1 SDK still ships the feature

questions.explanation: The deprecation SEP specifies a minimum window of at least twelve months, measured from the release of the revision that first marks the feature Deprecated. Expedited removal requires a published advisory or documented exploitation with no in-place mitigation, and must still leave at least ninety days.

questions.question: A client declares the Tasks extension; the server does not support it. What should happen?

options.text: The server falls back to core behaviour and returns an ordinary synchronous result
The server returns -32021, since a declared extension is a required capability
The server returns a CreateTaskResult anyway, which the client may ignore
The client must stop using the server until the extension is supported

questions.explanation: When one party supports an extension and the other does not, the supporting party MUST either revert to core protocol behaviour or reject the request if the extension is mandatory for it. Returning a task to a client that did not declare support is the mirror-image violation.

questions.question: A feature you depend on is marked Deprecated in the current revision. What can you rely on, and what should you plan?

options.text: It still works but servers may disable it at will; plan to migrate immediately
It has already stopped working in the current revision, so migrate before you upgrade at all
It still works and must keep working; plan the migration before the removal window opens
It works only for clients that explicitly opt in through a capability flag

questions.explanation: Deprecated means still normative and still functioning, with removal announced in advance — no sooner than twelve months, or ninety days for an expedited security removal. Removed is the state where it stops working.

questions.question: When was the HTTP+SSE transport deprecated?

options.text: 2025-11-25, the final revision of the legacy, handshake-based era
It is not deprecated: it remains the supported transport for older clients
2026-07-28, the same revision that deprecated Roots, Sampling and Logging
2025-03-26, when Streamable HTTP replaced it; 2026-07-28 only reclassified it

questions.explanation: HTTP+SSE has been deprecated since protocol version 2025-03-26. SEP-2596 reclassified it under the new feature-lifecycle policy, and its earliest removal is three months after that SEP reaches Final, unlike the twelve-month clock on features deprecated in 2026-07-28.

questions.question: Which of these was REMOVED outright in 2026-07-28 rather than deprecated?

options.text: The HTTP+SSE transport, whose removal clock started in 2025-03-26
Roots, which servers may still request through MRTR
Dynamic Client Registration, which remains as a fallback
The initialize handshake and notifications/initialized

questions.explanation: The handshake, protocol sessions and Mcp-Session-Id, ping, logging/setLevel, notifications/roots/list_changed, the GET stream, resources/subscribe and SSE resumability were removed by the revision. Roots, Sampling, Logging, DCR, includeContext values and HTTP+SSE are Deprecated, which means still present.

questions.question: Your server must serve both legacy clients and 2026-07-28 clients. What tells a request which era it belongs to?

options.text: The presence of a session id, which only modern clients send
The MCP-Protocol-Version header on the POST, with modern requests also carrying _meta
The first message, since only legacy clients open the exchange with an initialize request
The endpoint path, since each era is served on its own URL by convention

questions.explanation: The advertised revision in the MCP-Protocol-Version header is the signal, and modern requests additionally carry per-request _meta. Session ids and the initialize handshake were removed in 2026-07-28, so their absence is the rule and not an era marker.

questions.question: You still run the HTTP+SSE transport. What governs when you must be off it?

options.text: Removal comes three months after SEP-2596 reaches Final, not on a fixed calendar date
It has no removal plan; it stays Deprecated for as long as legacy clients exist
It was removed in 2026-07-28 already, so it is failing for modern clients now
Removal comes twelve months after the 2026-07-28 release, like every other deprecation

questions.explanation: HTTP+SSE has been Deprecated since 2025-03-26 and its removal is tied to a process milestone: three months after SEP-2596 is marked Final. The generic twelve-month floor covers the features deprecated in 2026-07-28.
